title: How SPAM Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore SPAM, the canned pork-and-ham product made by Hormel. They open with the 2010 Carnival Splendor cruise ship breakdown (the "Spamcation"), then cover what SPAM contains, its origin as Hormel spiced ham and the naming contest that produced the name, its boost from the Lend-Lease Act and World War Two, its popularity in Hawaii and Okinawa, production at the Austin, Minnesota and Fremont, Nebraska plants, the Spam Museum, nutrition and nitrite/cancer concerns, Monty Python's Spam sketch, the "spam" email term, Muppet Treasure Island's Sam the Eagle-style character Spam, a Hormel lawsuit, and a listener mail question about how the hosts share airtime.

segments.title: Opening banter and Carnival Splendor cruise story
segments.summary: The hosts joke around and recount the Carnival Splendor cruise ship losing power after an engine room fire, with passengers stranded for days and supplies including SPAM dropped by the US Navy. They tie this to the 'Spamcation' nickname and swap cruise anecdotes.

segments.title: What SPAM contains and shelf life
segments.summary: Chuck describes SPAM as pork shoulder and ham with salt, sugar, water, and a small amount of sodium nitrite, which Hormel says prevents botulism and keeps the meat pink. Hormel says the shelf life is indefinite but flavor declines over about three years.

segments.title: Origins: Hormel spiced ham and canning
segments.summary: Hormel's earlier product was spiced ham, which sold poorly because fresh meat was hard to differentiate. Jay Hormel, son of founder George Hormel, moved into canned meat in Austin, Minnesota during the Depression. Early canning struggled with meat cells breaking down, solved with salt, temperature control, and vacuum mixing. The hosts also discuss the old key-opening can.

segments.title: Naming SPAM
segments.summary: Jay Hormel's marketing included a twenty-piece Mexican band touring to promote chili. A name contest yielded weak entries, so at a New Year's Eve party guests were given free drinks for each name written. Kenneth Daniel, a Broadway actor, came up with the name SPAM and was reportedly paid one hundred dollars. The origin of the name is otherwise unclear, with various acronym theories.

segments.title: World War Two, Lend-Lease, and postwar popularity
segments.summary: The Lend-Lease Act let the US send food and supplies to countries fighting the Axis powers. Hormel shipped large amounts of SPAM, which became common for GIs in the Pacific and European theaters. Soldiers got tired of it, but many developed a taste for it after the war, and Hormel ran a postwar advertising campaign.

segments.title: SPAM in Hawaii, Okinawa, and Asia; Hormel labor history
segments.summary: SPAM is especially popular in Hawaii and Okinawa, linked to American military presence, and appears in dishes like SPAM musubi and on McDonald's and Burger King breakfast menus in Hawaii. The hosts also describe Jay Hormel's labor reforms, which earned him the nickname red capitalist from Fortune magazine.

segments.title: SPAM production process and Spam Museum
segments.summary: SPAM is made at plants in Austin, Minnesota and Fremont, Nebraska, with about thirteen workers per factory. Pork is machine-separated from bone, ham is trimmed by hand, the mix is ground, blended, piped into cans, sealed, and cooked in large cookers. Labels changed from lithography to plastic wrap. The Spam Museum in Austin is free and staffed partly by retired factory workers.

segments.title: Nutrition, sodium, and processed meat cancer concerns
segments.summary: A twelve-ounce can has six servings and about a full day's sodium; it is high in saturated fat. Reduced sodium and light versions exist. The hosts note a University of Hawaii study linking processed meat to pancreatic cancer risk, tied to nitrites forming nitrosamines; the FDA has not taken action. They also note that SPAM is a food for many low-income people.

segments.title: Pop culture: Monty Python, Muppets, Hormel lawsuit, and spam email
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Monty Python's Spam sketch, the Muppet Treasure Island character Spam and Hormel's lawsuit against the Jim Henson Company, and the origin of 'spam' for unwanted email from bulletin board and chat room flooding. They also cover the Waikiki Spam Jam festival and Richard LeFevre's record of eating eight cans in twelve minutes.

segments.title: Listener mail: how the hosts share airtime
segments.summary: Kristen from Toronto asks how Josh and Chuck divide speaking time evenly. They say it is equitable, that they watch for talking too much, and that they've outgrown fifth-grade-style turn fights.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts promote the How Stuff Works SPAM article, the site search bar, and the listener mail address, then sign off.
